title: Korach: sounds fair (Numbers 16:3)
hook: Korach says all the congregation is holy; the words are true, the motive is not

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzitzit, the fringes, and your line, see and remember. Did your knot remind you of something, and did you act on it? Hold on to those fringes. They come back today, in an argument. Day four hundred fifty-one.

A speech can be built entirely out of true sentences. Everyone deserves a voice. The people in charge have been there too long. Why should a few decide for everyone? A listener can agree with every word and still sense something off, once they notice who's speaking, and what that person would get if they won. This week's portion opens with exactly that kind of speech. It's delivered to Moses' face, in front of a crowd, by his own cousin. And the line at the center of it is hard to argue with.
screen: `A SPEECH MADE OF TRUE SENTENCES.` → `WHO'S SPEAKING?` → `MOSES' OWN COUSIN.`

segments.voice: Korach is a Levite, a grandson of Kohath, from the same family as Moses and Aaron. He gathers Dathan and Abiram, and two hundred fifty respected leaders, and they confront Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them; wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?" Every phrase has a source. At Sinai, God called the whole people a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. In Leviticus, holiness was spoken to the whole congregation. Korach's words echo the Torah back at Moses. So what's wrong? The rabbis looked under the speech. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says Korach was jealous: a younger cousin had been appointed leader of their clan instead of him. And a midrash pictures his opening move. He dresses his followers in cloaks made entirely of blue wool, and asks Moses: does a cloak that's all blue still need a blue thread in its fringes? Moses says yes. Korach's crowd laughs. A whole garment of blue, and you still need one thread? He's using yesterday's commandment to make both the law and Moses look ridiculous. Then Moses answers, and he exposes the motive. You Levites, he says, isn't it enough that you serve at the sanctuary? Now you want the priesthood too? Moses even hands Korach's words back to him: you take too much upon you. In the rabbis' reading, the claim was that everyone is equal. The goal was to be above.
screen: `ALL THE CONGREGATION ARE HOLY.` · `TRUE WORDS, FROM THE TORAH.` · `A CLOAK ALL OF BLUE.` · `NOW YOU WANT THE PRIESTHOOD TOO?` · then, large: `WHAT'S UNDER THE ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check your motive in one argument. Breathe, and bring to mind a disagreement you're in right now: at work, at home, online. Say your position to yourself in its best words. Then ask, quietly: what do I get if I win? Respect? Being right? A seat I've wanted? Revenge for an old slight? Don't judge what you find. Just look under the argument, the way the rabbis looked under Korach's. Notice whether the words and the want point the same way. The bell holds the time.
Korach. The Levite who said all the congregation is holy, true words, carried by a wish to be above them.
Your line: what's under the argument. Today, before you make your next point in a disagreement, name to yourself what you want from winning. Day four hundred fifty-one.

screen: `DAY 451 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KORACH: NOT FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE (AVOT 5:17).`

howItsDone: When the portion Korach is read, Jewish teachers often pair Korach's speech with the midrash of the all-blue cloak, and use it to talk about the difference between a true claim and the reason someone is making it.

myth: Korach's claim that all the people are holy has no basis in the Torah
at Sinai the people are called a holy nation; his words echo the Torah.
Rashi says Korach was jealous of a cousin's appointment
a younger cousin was made leader of their clan.
Moses used Korach's own phrase against him
you take too much upon you, Moses says back.

fork.setup: you're Moses. Korach's crowd wears cloaks all of blue and asks: does a cloak that's entirely blue still need a blue thread in its fringes? what do you answer?
fork.reveal: in the midrash Moses says yes, and Korach's crowd laughs. the question was built to make the law look silly, not to learn it.

original.note: Hebrew: you take too much upon you. Korach's charge, and Moses' answer back.

trapdoor: what you thought: Korach was a villain with a bad argument.
what it means: his argument quoted the Torah; the problem was what he wanted from it.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on Numbers 16:1 traces the revolt to jealousy over Elizaphan's appointment as prince of the Kohathites in Numbers 3:30.

sources.quoted: Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them; wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?

sources.ref: Rashi on Numbers 16:1; Midrash Tanchuma, Korach 2; Numbers Rabbah 18

notes: Numbers 16:3 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; confirm.
Korach's lineage: son of Izhar son of Kohath (Exodus 6:18–21), so a first cousin of Moses and Aaron; the script says 'a grandson of Kohath, from the same family'. Confirm.
The all-blue cloak midrash (Tanchuma Korach 2; Numbers Rabbah 18:3; cited by Rashi on 16:1); confirm citations.
Moses' 'you take too much upon you, ye sons of Levi' is Numbers 16:7; 'seek ye the priesthood also' is 16:10. Paraphrased.

Review pass: 'a younger cousin' means Elizaphan son of Uzziel, Kohath's youngest son (Korach's father Izhar was the second). The jealousy motive and the 'true words, wrong motive' framing in the hook are the rabbinic reading (Rashi, Tanchuma), not the plain text alone; the teach attributes them to the rabbis. Confirm.
